name: RCA (phono) jack
ascii:
shield / ground (sleeve)      center pin (signal)
          |                             |
     =====[=============================(o)===>   (plug ->)
          |                             |
        outer                         center
     (0 V return)                   (audio / video)
description: The ubiquitous single-signal AV connector: a center pin for the signal and an outer sleeve for ground/shield -- one connector carries one unbalanced channel. Color coding is convention only (white/red = left/right analog audio, yellow = composite video, orange = S/PDIF digital, etc.); electrically they're all identical RCA jacks.

contacts.name: SIGNAL
contacts.description: the signal conductor -- line-level audio, composite video, or S/PDIF depending on use

contacts.name: SHIELD
contacts.description: outer sleeve: ground / shield / 0 V return

variants: Colour is convention, not function: white=L, red=R (analog audio); yellow=composite video; red/green/blue=component video; orange=coaxial S/PDIF. All are the same RCA connector -- a video signal happily runs down a 'red audio' cable.
S/PDIF over RCA is a 75-ohm coaxial digital link; using a normal (non-75-ohm) analog audio RCA cable for it usually works over short runs but can cause dropouts on longer ones.
gotchas: RCA is UNBALANCED (signal + ground, no differential), so it picks up hum and noise over long runs -- fine for a rack, poor for stage-length cables (that's what XLR/TRS-balanced is for).
The sleeve makes contact first and breaks last, so hot-plugging thumps: connect RCA cables with the volume down.
It's a single channel per connector -- stereo needs two, and composite video + stereo audio needs three.
notes: RCA / phono: center pin = signal, sleeve = ground. Colour coding is convention only. Universal.
